title: Expertise: The Best Professional Investment You Can Make
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that the most resilient professional investment for educators is deep expertise, because classrooms, curricula, and methodologies are all subject to reassignment or disruption while genuine competence travels with the person. He grounds expertise-building in a clear conception of education's essential goal — the promotion of long-term flourishing of young people through teaching them toward mastery — and presents this Everest as the stable orientation point that makes policy turbulence navigable. The article refines the common 'it's all about the kids' framing, arguing that it is both too narrow (the specific goal is mastery-based flourishing) and too narrow in another sense (teacher flourishing is equally necessary to achieve it). Stuart models how expertise compounds: by committing in 2014 to six interconnected domains, he has accumulated over a decade of deepening insight that continues to grow. The piece closes with an invitation for educators to identify their own focused investment areas and commit to digging deeper into them year after year.
points: Expertise is the most resilient professional asset because it cannot be reassigned or dismantled by policy — unlike classrooms, curricula, or methodologies.

Education's essential goal — long-term flourishing of young people through growth toward mastery — is the fixed Everest that makes the ever-changing policy landscape navigable rather than disorienting.
'It's all about the kids' is both too narrow and too broad: the specific goal is mastery-based flourishing, and achieving it requires attending to teacher flourishing as well.
A focused investment in a small number of connected expertise domains — Stuart chose six — compounds over time, delivering deepening insight that continues to grow even after a decade of practice.

Rigorous testing of answers is required at every stage: rushing into conclusions wastes time and frustrates development, while patient inquiry into the right questions yields durable professional growth.
quotes: The most resilient thing you can build for yourself as a professional educator isn't a beautiful classroom (those can get reassigned) or an iron-clad curriculum (we've seen how quickly the winds of policy can reduce these to rubble) or a foolproof methodology (looking at you, AI).

you reduce education down to its essential goal, its enduring Everest: the promotion of the long-term flourishing of young people through the means of teaching them to master things. This part is critical — if you don't bring your mind back to this, again and again, you'll get frustrated by the ever-present winds of change.

it's not "all about the kids" — it's both narrower and broader than that. Narrower in the sense that it's all about advancing the long-term flourishing of young people by teaching them toward mastery. Broader in that to achieve the goal, I need to attend not just to their long-term flourishing but also to mine.

you start asking the next obvious questions: how can classes or schools or grade levels like mine best support the long-term flourishing via growth toward mastery of young people? All answers must be tested. These are the places to be rigorous.
Over time, you identify a few key answers to the question of long-term flourishing in our setting, and you resolve to dig deeper and deeper into them, year after year.

What I like about this list is that it's manageable. I don't need to blow things up to get better at any of these. I can weave this stuff in to any subject, any curriculum, any setting. And I also appreciate that, over a decade later, I'm still learning loads each year about how they work, how to improve, how to be more productive and humane.
